faq.a: Water forms a slippery layer between the tyre and the road, so less rubber actually touches the surface. Less contact means less grip for steering and braking.
asks: Why do cars skid in the rain?

faq.q: How do tyre grooves clear water?
faq.a: As the tyre rolls, each groove fills with water that is squeezed out of the contact patch and flung out to the sides and behind, leaving the rubber blocks in contact with the road.
On a dry track a smooth slick tyre puts the most rubber on the road for the best grip. In the rain slicks would aquaplane, so racers switch to grooved wet tyres.
asks: Why do Formula 1 cars use slick tyres?

faq.a: Aquaplaning is when a tyre rides up on a layer of water and loses contact with the road. The steering goes light and braking does little. Ease off the accelerator gently and do not brake hard or steer sharply.
asks: What should you do if you aquaplane?

faq.q: What is the legal minimum tread depth?
faq.a: In the UK and the EU, car tyres must have at least 1.6 millimetres of tread across the central three quarters of the tyre. Wet grip falls noticeably well before that.
asks: How deep should tyre tread be?

facts: The legal minimum tread depth for car tyres in the UK and EU is 1.6 millimetres.
The tiny slits cut into tread blocks are called sipes.
Slick racing tyres have no tread because on a dry track more rubber contact means more grip.
